The driving-force match uses single representative close-hauled points (beta~25-27 deg). A proper VPP sweep across TWA would give the area ratio as a function of point of sail; on a reach the area advantage of the wing shrinks because both rigs run higher driving coefficients.
Aspect ratio, vertical area distribution between the two masts, and mast-interference (biplane downwash) are not modeled here and will move the per-mast area and the balance-axis location.

Center-of-pressure migration with camber/rotation for the SOFT (cambered, asymmetric-on-tack) configuration differs from the clean symmetric 0.25c assumption; the balance axis should be tuned to the cambered operating CoP, not the symmetric one.

research.topic: Aerodynamic interaction of two fore-and-aft wingmasts (slot effect, tandem/biplane theory, independent-AoA steering & depower) for a sailboat with two independently rotatable free-rotating wingsails
research.summary: Two rigs spaced fore-and-aft interact through their circulation fields, not through a Venturi "nozzle." Gentry's modern sail theory (validated repeatedly by RANS CFD) shows the FORWARD sail (jib analog) heads the flow at the AFT sail (main analog) and, via opposing circulation in the slot, REDUCES lee-side peak suction on the aft sail — delaying its separation and letting it run at higher AoA. The aft sail in turn raises the upwash and leech-region velocity at the forward sail, increasing the forward sail's circulation and lift. Net result: the two-sail system makes more total lift than the sum of the isolated sails, and the system points higher. Classical multiplane theory (Munk's stagger theorem) says induced drag depends on the GAP/SPAN ratio and the inter-element lift ratio, NOT on streamwise stagger, so the fore/aft spacing is essentially free to optimize for circulation interaction, helm balance, and structure rather than for induced drag. For two surfaces at the same height (a true streamwise tandem, which is the wingmast case), classical biplane theory gives minimum induced drag as gap/span -> large; for the in-plane circulation-interaction benefit the useful working separation is on the order of ~1 chord between rig axes, with the interaction decaying as separation grows. A systematic low-Re two-wing experiment (Jones, Cleaver & Gursul 2015) found total-lift ratios up to RL≈1.3 over a single wing, that the true "tandem" regime begins at streamwise stagger ΔX/c >= 1, and that in true tandem the LEADING wing carries the larger share of lift while the trailing wing (sitting in the leader's wake/downwash) carries less — directly mapping the schooner/AC observation that the forward rig is the more powerful, more highly loaded sail upwind. Independent AoA control of the two rigs is a powerful steering and power/depower mechanism: differential trim shifts the combined center-of-effort fore/aft (steers, like a schooner shifting CE to add/remove weather helm) and lets either rig be feathered/depowered independently (like AC multi-element twist control). Recommended rig-axis spacing: ~1.0-2.0 chord lengths (gap/chord 1-2); ~1c maximizes circulation coupling/pointing but courts wake interference and backwinding of the aft rig at high load, ~2c is a safer, more independent, more steering-authoritative spacing. Load implication: upwind, the forward (windward-most-exposed, clean-air) rig generally sees the higher aero load; the aft rig is partially shadowed and de-rated, and over-sheeting the forward rig backwinds and unloads the aft rig.

findings.claim: The jib-mainsail 'slot effect' is a circulation interaction, NOT a Venturi nozzle. The forward sail produces a 'header' on the aft sail and, via opposing circulation in the slot, REDUCES (not increases) the velocity / peak suction on the lee side of the aft sail, delaying its separation.
findings.value: Gentry: 'the primary effect of the jib is to reduce the velocities on the lee side of the mainsail... reduction in the pressure gradient... lessen the possibility of lee side separation.' The two circulation fields 'tend to oppose each other in the slot.' The old venturi/speed-up explanation 'is completely wrong' because higher slot speed would INCREASE separation risk, opposite to observed behavior (oversheeting the jib backwinds/luffs the main).
findings.source: Arvel Gentry, 'A Review of Modern Sail Theory' / 'The Origins of Lift' (full text extracted); corroborated by Wilkinson/Richards 'slot effect revisited' RANS CFD (ScienceDirect S016761050900066X) and giornaledellavela summaries

findings.claim: The aft sail (main) increases the forward sail's (jib's) lift: it raises upwash at the forward sail's luff (point higher) and puts the forward sail's leech in a high-velocity region, so the forward sail returns to a higher base velocity than if isolated -> higher circulation, higher lift, less separation on the forward sail.
findings.value: Gentry: jib leech 'is in a high-speed flow region created by the mainsail... the jib will have a much higher pressure difference across the fabric and higher lift'; mainsail upwash shifts jib stagnation point to windward so the boat 'can be pointed closer to the wind without the jib stalling.'
findings.source: Gentry, 'A Review of Modern Sail Theory' (sections 10.1-10.2)

findings.claim: Two sails working together produce more TOTAL lift than the sum of the two sails operating alone (synergistic augmentation), and the gap between them is a key determinant of total lift/thrust.
findings.value: 'The combination of two sails produces the lift force larger than the sum of that produced separately by each sail and the gap distance between the two sails is an important factor to determine total lift and thrust.' In a measured trim sweep, easing main twist changed driving-force coeff CX from 0.33->0.39 (~18%) and side-force CY from 1.16->1.39 (~20%), illustrating the magnitude of trim/interaction sensitivity.
findings.source: RANS CFD sail-interaction studies (ScienceDirect S016761050900066X; ResearchGate 232809374); IntechOpen 'Sail Performance Analysis...' (Fujin sea-trial + VLM/CFD, twist-sweep numbers extracted)

findings.claim: Munk's stagger theorem: for a multiplane the induced drag is INDEPENDENT of the streamwise position (stagger) of the lifting elements, provided the gap/span ratios and element-to-element lift ratios are held fixed. So fore/aft spacing of the two rigs is essentially free to choose for circulation coupling, helm balance, and structure rather than being set by induced-drag minimization.
findings.value: Induced drag is a function of gap/span and inter-element lift split, not stagger. Empirically, positive stagger + larger gap give higher lift-curve slope and lower induced drag than negative stagger / small gap (lift distributions then no longer identical, so the strict theorem's assumption is relaxed).
findings.source: NASA NTRS 19760003933 'Trim Drag in the Light of Munk's Stagger Theorem'; ResearchGate 'Gap and Stagger Effects on Biplanes' (269062106) and invariant-formulation Munk augmentation (259334570)

findings.claim: Optimal SPACING for the in-plane circulation/biplane benefit is on the order of ~1 chord. Classical biplane theory gives minimum induced drag at gap/chord ~= 1 (for co-planar wings); tandem-wing studies find total lift maximized near ~1.0 chord spacing while thrust/propulsion benefit peaks nearer ~0.5 chord. Interaction strength decays as spacing grows.
findings.value: 'lowest induced drag... two wings placed on the same level with a gap-to-chord ratio equal to 1'; 'Total lift by tandem wings was maximized at a wing spacing of 1.0 chord length, while thrust was maximized at a spacing of 0.5.' Gains 'become smaller as the stagger distance increases owing to weakened airfoil-to-airfoil interference.'
findings.source: Tandem-wing reviews (ResearchGate 268558153, 279169936); flapping-tandem optimization literature. NOTE these mix gap (vertical) and stagger (streamwise) conventions

findings.claim: Quantified two-wing lift augmentation: a systematic low-Re experiment found total-lift ratios up to RL ~ 1.12 (biplane, zero stagger) and up to RL ~ 1.3 with stagger, with stall delayed from ~15deg to ~25-30deg. The 'true tandem' regime (streamwise) begins at stagger ratio ΔX/c >= 1.
findings.value: Max total-lift ratio RL = 1.32 +/-0.04 at ΔX/c=0.5, ΔY/c=0.85, alpha=25deg; RL=1.27 at ΔX/c=1; RL=1.18 at ΔX/c=1.5 -> max achievable lift augmentation DECREASES as streamwise stagger grows. 'tandem state is only true for ΔX/c >= 1.' Best power-efficiency: +20% at ΔX/c=0.5, ΔY/c=0.85, alpha=25deg.
findings.source: Jones, Cleaver & Gursul, 'Aerodynamics of biplane and tandem wings at low Reynolds numbers', Experiments in Fluids 2015 (Bath ePrint full text extracted)

findings.claim: Which rig is more highly loaded: in the TRUE tandem regime (ΔX/c >= 1) the LEADING wing always produces greater lift than the trailing wing; the trailing wing sits in the leader's wake/downwash and is de-rated. (Only in the quasi-biplane regime ΔX/c=0.5 can the trailing wing transiently exceed the leader for a band of vertical gaps.)
findings.value: 'With ΔX/c = 1... the leading wing always produces greater lift than the trailing wing.' Example direct-tandem (ΔY/c=0): leading CL1=0.62-0.66 vs trailing CL2=0.02-0.23. Trailing wing also shows much larger lift FLUCTUATION (unsteady stall switching) -> a fatigue/buffet consideration for the aft mast.
findings.source: Jones, Cleaver & Gursul 2015 (full text); consistent with Gentry/schooner observation that the forward sail is the more powerful upwind sail

findings.claim: Independent AoA control of two rigs steers the boat by shifting the combined center-of-effort fore/aft relative to the hull's center of lateral resistance (the schooner/ketch CE-balance mechanism), and depowers by feathering/twisting either rig independently (the AC multi-element mechanism).
findings.value: Schooner practice: 'reefing the main or furling the jib are versatile ways to move the center of effort... furling the main, the CE adjusts forward; furling the jib, CE moves aft' -> trims weather/lee helm. Differential rig trim is the wing analog: load the forward rig to drive the bow down/add lee-helm-correcting moment, load the aft rig for weather helm. AC wings depower by one-button twist that spills the upper sections.
findings.source: Schooner-rig & helm-balance sources (firgelliauto, goodoldboat, SailZing, Wikipedia weather-helm); AC wing twist control (maritime-executive, yachtingworld AC podcast)

findings.claim: Prior art for two/multiple independently controlled wing-type rigs exists: schooners (split fore/main with slot), AC72/AC-class two-element wings with 8 independently twistable flap sections, free-rotating self-trimming wingsails (Atlantis Prindle-19 with flying-tail control about a stub mast), twin automated rotating inflatable wingsails (MODX 70ft cat), and explicit 'free-wing' tandem proposals using a small downstream wing on a lever to set the upstream wing's AoA with independent flap angles for steering.
findings.value: MODX: 'twin inflatable rotating wingsails set on telescopic retractable masts'; free-wing editorial: 'independent steering control would allow each downstream wing flap to be set at a different angle relative to the main propulsion wing-sail'; AC flap 'divided vertically into eight independent sections'; Aeroforce dual rig claims '35% extra power over conventional sails.'
findings.source: maritime-executive free-wing & AC-wing features; yachtingworld MODX; americansailing wingsail; sailingscuttlebutt dual-wingsail; Wikipedia Wingsail (USA-17)

findings.claim: RECOMMENDED rig-axis spacing for two wingmasts: roughly 1.0-2.0 chord lengths (separation/chord 1-2). ~1c maximizes circulation coupling, mutual upwash and pointing but risks wake impingement and backwinding/unsteady stall of the aft rig at high load; ~2c gives cleaner, more independent rigs with stronger differential-trim steering authority at modest loss of mutual augmentation. Practical wingsail/schooner experience and the tandem data both place the useful window in this band; below ~1c interference and aft-rig buffet dominate, above ~2-3c the interaction (and the synergistic lift bonus) fades toward two isolated rigs.
findings.value: Synthesis: classical co-planar biplane optimum gap/chord ~1; tandem total-lift peak ~1c spacing; augmentation decays and aft-rig unsteadiness grows toward the small-gap end; Munk theorem frees streamwise spacing from induced-drag penalty so the choice is governed by interaction + helm authority + structure.
findings.source: Synthesis of Munk theorem (NASA), Jones/Cleaver/Gursul 2015, classical biplane gap/chord~1, tandem-wing reviews, and schooner/AC practice

derived_numbers.how: Synthesis: classical co-planar biplane min-induced-drag gap/chord~1, tandem total-lift peak near 1c, interaction decay & aft-rig buffet growth below ~1c, fade-out beyond ~2-3c; Munk theorem removes induced-drag penalty on streamwise spacing so it is chosen for interaction + helm balance + structure

open_questions: Reynolds-number and thickness gap: the cleanest quantitative tandem dataset (Jones/Cleaver/Gursul) is thin flat-plate wings at Re=1e5; CFRP wingmasts run at far higher Re with thick cambered sections. The qualitative regimes should hold but the augmentation magnitudes and optimal gap need re-derivation at the design Re/section (a CFD or panel-method sweep in this repo).

Free-rotation coupling: with BOTH rigs free to weathervane and only their tails/AoA set, the upwash/header from each rig changes the LOCAL apparent-wind direction seen by the other. Does this make the two free-rotating rigs aerodynamically coupled/unstable, and what tail-volume / AoA-authority is needed to hold a commanded differential AoA against the partner rig's induced flow?

Optimal spacing under heel and at off-design AWA: the ~1-2c recommendation is for upwind, level. Downwind the rigs may want to be separated/staggered laterally to avoid full shadowing; quantify how the load split and optimal gap move with apparent wind angle and heel.

Quantified steering authority: how much fore/aft CE shift (as a fraction of waterline/CLR lead) is achievable purely by differential rig AoA before either rig stalls or backwinds — i.e., can the boat be steered/trimmed in a useful envelope WITHOUT a rudder, as the free-wing prior art implies?

Aft-rig buffet/fatigue: the trailing rig shows much larger lift fluctuation (stall-switching) in the tandem data. Quantify the unsteady-load spectrum on the aft mast at the chosen spacing for the fatigue/structural sizing path, since the aft mast may be fatigue- rather than peak-load-driven.

Whether to deliberately stagger heights/decalage (vertical gap, decalage angle) to recover the higher RL~1.3 augmentation that the data show requires non-zero vertical gap — at the cost of asymmetric structure and a higher combined CE.

research.topic: Wind environment and survival load case for a free-standing CFRP sailboat wingmast (60 ft cruiser); operational reefing schedule vs bare weathervaned hurricane survival
research.summary: For a 60 ft cruiser, the first reef goes in around 15-18 kt apparent wind, second reef ~20-25 kt, third reef / storm trysail by ~30-35 kt — the reefing schedule deliberately CAPS the rig aerodynamic force so the operational base bending moment stays roughly bounded (estimated ~120-150 kN.m at the reef-down boundaries for an assumed 25 m mast / ~160 m^2 sail / ~11 m heeling arm). Dynamic pressure q=0.5*rho*V^2 (rho=1.225) ranges from ~65 Pa at 20 kt to ~1.62 kPa at 100 kt and ~3.04 kPa at 137 kt (Cat 5). The brief's SURVIVAL scenario is a bare wingmast (no soft sail) left fully weathervaned in hurricane wind. A reasonable design wind is hurricane Cat 3, ~100 kt 1-min sustained (Saffir-Simpson Cat 1 begins at 64 kt, Cat 3 at 96-112 kt, Cat 5 at >=137 kt); 3-s gusts add ~1.3x on V => ~1.7x on q. DNV-ST-0412 (large yacht rigs) frames rig design around an operational apparent wind AWS0 and applies reserve factors RF>=4.5 (Cat I) on design load and RF>=3.1 on mast-panel compression, rather than naming a single survival wind. KEY RESULT: if the vane were PERFECT (pure drag at 0 deg AoA, streamlined foil), the survival moment is trivial — only ~5-15 kN.m at 100 kt — far below operational. But survival is NOT pure drag: imperfect weathervaning (vane lag, shifting gust direction, VIV/galloping) puts the mast at a non-zero effective AoA, and then the LARGE chord (planform) area generates a lift-type side force at Cl up to ~1.0-1.2. That off-axis side-force case dominates: ~355-426 kN.m at 100 kt (Cat 3) and ~666-799 kN.m at 137 kt (Cat 5), i.e. ~2.8x to ~5.3x the operational case. CONCLUSION: the survival (bare weathervaned, off-axis side-force) case GOVERNS the structural design, but only because a free wing presents its full chord area off-axis — the pure-drag idealization badly under-predicts and must not be used. VIV lock-in is a secondary concern: at St=0.18 on the ~0.2 m thickness scale the shedding frequency (~9-28 Hz at 20-60 kt) sits well above a likely mast first-bending mode (~0.5-1.5 Hz), so classical resonant lock-in is unlikely in survival winds; the governing mechanism is the quasi-static gust-yaw side force, with galloping as a tail risk for the (stalled, bluff-behaving) fat section.

findings.claim: First reef typically at ~15-18 kt apparent wind upwind for a cruiser; lighter boats nearer 15, heavier offshore boats 20+. A common simple schedule: first reef 15 kt, second reef 20 kt.

findings.source: Yachting Monthly 'Essential reefing tips'; YBW Forum

This is ~2.8x-5.3x the operational sailing moment, so survival GOVERNS.

open_questions: Actual exposed mast height, mean chord, thickness (t/c) and mass distribution of the design wingmast — all moments scale linearly with A and arm, so these dimensions set the absolute numbers; current values are representative placeholders.

What effective off-axis AoA / Cl should be assumed for an imperfectly weathervaned free wing in a hurricane? This is the single biggest driver of the governing survival moment and deserves CFD or wind-tunnel data on the actual section (lift slope, Clmax, stall behavior, and post-stall galloping tendency for the fat section).

Does the design intent allow the wingmast to be LOCKED (not free) or feathered/depowered in survival, or is free-rotation mandatory? A free vane that can lag or oscillate is the worst case; a lockable/parked orientation could collapse the survival load toward the trivial pure-drag value.

Atmospheric boundary-layer wind shear and gust spectrum at the site/anchorage — using a sheared profile lowers the force centroid and the moment vs the uniform-wind assumption used here; specify a design wind profile (e.g. power-law alpha).

Exact DNV-ST-0412 / ABS load convention to adopt: confirm whether to size to AWS0 with RF>=4.5 (operational basis) or to an explicit survival wind with a separate (lower) reserve factor — the standard's full text was not machine-readable in this session.

Galloping/VIV check on the ACTUAL section: confirm the first few structural natural frequencies of the as-designed CFRP mast and recheck Den Hartog galloping stability and any low-wind lock-in, since the fat bluff section behaves unlike a thin streamlined strut.

research.topic: Prior art and engineering norms for free-standing (unstayed) composite masts and analogous tapered cantilever composite structures (wind-turbine blade roots, tapered tubular cantilevers) — loads, deflection, taper, wall/diameter trends, safety factors, rotating-mast bearings, and failure modes
research.summary: A free-standing mast is engineered as a vertical tapered cantilever (vs. a stayed mast, which is a compression column): wind/sail load bends it, and there is no rigging to react that bending, so the tube itself must carry the full bending moment. The governing design load across the field is the boat's maximum righting moment (the most the hull can deliver before it heels away), applied at the optimal-beating heel angle, and the maximum bending moment occurs at the deck partners (the cantilever root / fulcrum). The dominant marine practice (Eric Sponberg, who designed ~60 free-standing spars at Tillotson-Pearson/Freedom Yachts) uses a factor of safety of 3.0 on the laminate: either multiply the max righting-moment load by 3 against full laminate strength, or divide full strength by 3 to get allowables. Laminate layup is fiber-steered to the load: roughly 60-80% (typ. ~75%) of plies axial/0° to carry bending, with the remainder split between ±45° bias (torsion/shear) and 90° hoop (local-buckling and crush resistance) — about 12% ±45° and the balance 90% in one cited braid recipe. The laminate is thickest at the base and tapers toward the tip where moment goes to zero. A key thin-shell guard is a minimum wall-thickness-to-diameter ratio of about 3-4% (Sponberg) to resist local shell buckling; bamboo/natural analogs run 5-15%. Slenderness is held to L/r <= ~100 for marine cantilevers (steel column practice allows up to 120). Mast "bury" (penetration below deck, distance between the two bearings) follows roughly a 1-in-7 rule of mast-height-above-deck; a longer bury reduces the bearing-couple loads. For ROTATING free-standing masts (wingmasts, AeroRig/balestron), the bending moment is reacted as a force couple across two journal bearings — an upper bearing at the deck partners and a lower bearing at the heel step — typically built as a fixed inner stub mast carrying two large bearings (aluminum/stainless bodies with Torlon or steel rollers/balls) over which the outer mast slips and freely rotates 360 deg. On a measured AeroRig with 1.9 m bury, the couple was ~34 tonnes at the deck-head bearing and ~28.4 tonnes at the heel — a vivid demonstration that bearing loads = moment / bury. Tip deflection is treated as a normal, visible operating characteristic (Freedom masts bend noticeably in puffs) rather than a hard serviceability limit; marine practice sizes on strength (FoS 3 on the righting-moment moment) and checks deflection/luff-curve for sail trim rather than enforcing a single published % limit. The strongest quantified deflection-limit analog is wind-turbine blades, which ARE strictly deflection-governed: IEC 61400 requires that under factored worst-case load the blade-tip-to-tower clearance not be reduced by more than ~30% of the unloaded gap (i.e. factored tip deflection <= ~70% of static clearance, via gamma_f x gamma_m x gamma_n). Wind-turbine composite blades and free-standing masts converge on very similar effective safety: blade ultimate uses a load factor gamma_f ~1.25-1.35 times a combined composite material factor gamma_m of ~2.45-2.94 (product of sub-factors for cure/temperature/aging/manufacturing — e.g. C2a=1.5 creep, C3a=1.1 temperature, C4a=1.1 prepreg or 1.2 hand-layup), plus a consequence factor gamma_n — yielding effective ultimate margins of roughly 3-4x on coupon strength, bracketing the marine FoS=3. Failure modes for thin CFRP shells in bending: (1) laminate strength — fiber compression/tension and matrix failure on the bending extreme fibers, screened with Tsai-Wu / Hashin / max-strain; (2) local shell buckling (short-wavelength wrinkling of the thin compression-side wall — the reason for the >=3-4% wall/diameter floor and hoop plies) and (3) global Euler-type column/cantilever buckling for very slender spars. A documented real-world Freedom-mast issue was brittle gelcoat circumferential surface cracking over un-cross-linked hoop-glass windings — worst near the gooseneck where bending stress is highest — a surface/cosmetic and manufacturing defect that generally did NOT penetrate the structural carbon, underscoring that bending stress peaks low on the spar and that ply-drop/surface detailing matters.

findings.claim: A free-standing mast is engineered as a cantilever (it bends), whereas a stayed mast is a column (it compresses); the unstayed tube must itself carry the full bending load from sail pressure with no rigging to react it.
findings.value: Cantilever vs. column distinction; carbon used because it is ~60% the weight of aluminum yet >2x as strong
findings.source: Eric Sponberg, 'Free-Standing Masts: State of the Art' (ericwsponberg.com PDF)

findings.claim: Maximum bending moment in a free-standing mast occurs at the deck partners, which act as the cantilever root / fulcrum; the heel step reacts a 'prying' load. The mast is supported in bending by the deck collar (partners) and the mast step.
findings.value: Max moment at partners (deck level); step takes prying/reaction load
findings.source: smalltridesign.com mast-design and Rigging-Mast-Loads pages; goodoldboat.com 'No Visible Means of Support'

findings.claim: The governing design load for a free-standing mast is the boat's maximum righting moment, evaluated at the heel angle for optimal beating in a good breeze; design packages predict deflection and luff curve from this.
findings.value: Design load = max righting moment (heeled)
findings.source: smalltridesign.com mast design; Sponberg state-of-the-art PDF (multihull max RM at windward-hull-fly)

findings.claim: Marine free-standing-spar practice uses a factor of safety of 3.0 on the laminate: multiply the max righting-moment load by 3 against full laminate strength, OR divide full strength properties by 3 to get allowable stresses.
findings.value: FoS = 3.0 (ultimate vs. operational max-RM load)
findings.source: Eric Sponberg via Scribd 'Design Engineering Masts' summary / proboat profile

findings.claim: Laminate is fiber-steered: most plies run axial (0deg) to carry bending; remainder is off-axis split between hoop (90deg) and bias (+/-45deg). The laminate is thickest at the base and tapers in thickness toward the tip where load goes to zero.
findings.value: 60-80% axial 0deg, 20-40% off-axis (split 90deg hoop + -/+45deg bias); one braided recipe ~75% axial / 12% +/-45 / rest 90
findings.source: Sponberg state-of-the-art PDF; smalltridesign Rigging-Mast-Loads page

findings.claim: Minimum wall-thickness-to-diameter ratio for carbon free-standing masts is about 3-4% (a thin-shell local-buckling guard). Natural/bamboo analogs use 5-15%. The Scribd Sponberg doc cites a 3% minimum wall/diameter ratio.
findings.value: wall/diameter >= ~3-4% (carbon); 5-15% for bamboo
findings.source: smalltridesign.com mast-design (citing Sponberg); Scribd 'Design Engineering Masts' summary

findings.claim: Slenderness (effective length / radius of gyration) is held to L/r <= ~100 for marine free-standing cantilevers; general steel column practice allows up to 120. Buckling FoS in this context cited as 1.5 (cruising) up to ~3.
findings.value: L/r <= 100 (marine); buckling FoS 1.5-3
findings.source: smalltridesign.com mast-design-01

findings.claim: Rotating free-standing masts (wingmast / AeroRig) react the bending moment as a force couple across two journal bearings: an upper bearing at the deck partners and a lower bearing at the heel step. Built as a fixed inner stub mast carrying two large bearings over which the outer mast slips and rotates 360deg.
findings.value: Two-bearing couple: partners (upper) + heel step (lower); inner stub-mast + outer rotating sleeve
findings.source: Sponberg state-of-the-art PDF (Wobegone Daze wingmast); sailingcatamarans.com AeroRig FAQ

findings.claim: On a measured AeroRig with 1.9 m mast bury (bearing spacing), the reaction couple was ~34 tonnes at the deck-head bearing and ~28.4 tonnes at the heel — i.e. bearing load = bending moment / bury distance, so a longer bury lowers bearing loads.
findings.value: 1.9 m bury -> 34 t deck bearing, 28.4 t heel bearing
findings.source: oceannavigator.com / sailmagazine.com Carbospars AeroRig data

findings.claim: Mast bury (penetration below deck / bearing spacing) follows roughly a 1-in-7 rule of mast height above deck: a 35 ft mast needs ~5 ft of bury.
findings.value: bury ~= 1/7 of above-deck height
findings.source: sailingcatamarans.com AeroRig/balestron FAQ

findings.claim: Wingmast rotating bearings are made with aluminum (or stainless) bodies and Torlon roller/ball elements; all-stainless rollers run harder/turn easier under load but cost more (~$3k vs ~$5k each). Masts in full bearings can be over-rotated freely 360deg.
findings.value: Aluminum/Torlon or all-stainless bearings; ~$3k-5k each
findings.source: Sponberg state-of-the-art PDF (Wobegone Daze)

findings.claim: Tip deflection on free-standing masts is treated as a normal, visible operating characteristic (masts bend noticeably in puffs), not a single hard % limit; marine practice sizes on strength (FoS 3 on max-RM) and checks deflection only for sail luff-curve/trim.
findings.value: No universal published % tip-deflection limit in marine spar practice; deflection is a sail-trim/serviceability check, not the sizing driver
findings.source: practical-sailor.com Freedom 36; goodoldboat.com; smalltridesign

findings.claim: The strongest quantified deflection-limit analog is wind-turbine blades: IEC 61400 requires that under factored worst-case load the blade-tip-to-tower clearance not be reduced by more than ~30% of the unloaded gap (factored tip deflection <= ~70% of static clearance), via gamma_f x gamma_m x gamma_n applied to characteristic deflection.
findings.value: Blade tip clearance reduction <= ~30% under factored load (IEC 61400-1 sec 7.6.5)
findings.source: IEC 61400-1 ed.3 sec 7.6.5 (via NREL/NWTC forum, ScienceDirect blade-tower clearance studies)

findings.claim: Wind-turbine composite blade ultimate strength uses a load partial factor gamma_f of ~1.25-1.35 times a combined material partial factor gamma_m of ~2.45-2.94 (product of sub-factors: e.g. creep C2a=1.5, temperature C3a=1.1, manufacturing C4a=1.1 prepreg / 1.2 hand layup), plus a consequence factor gamma_n.
findings.value: gamma_f ~1.25-1.35; combined gamma_m ~2.45-2.94 on coupon strength; effective ultimate margin ~3-4x
findings.source: NREL CP-440-23257 'Using Partial Safety Factors'; IEC 61400-1 ed.4 background doc; Sandia/OSTI blade composite reports

findings.claim: Failure modes for thin CFRP shells in bending: (1) laminate strength — fiber/matrix failure on the bending extreme fibers, screened by Tsai-Wu / Hashin / max-strain; (2) local shell buckling (short-wavelength compression-side wall wrinkling) — the reason for the 3-4% wall/diameter floor and hoop plies; (3) global Euler column/cantilever buckling for slender spars.
findings.value: Laminate strength (Tsai-Wu/Hashin), local shell buckling, global Euler buckling
findings.source: Sponberg state-of-the-art PDF (buckling for columns/cantilevers); composite design literature; project CLAUDE.md buckling conventions

findings.claim: A documented Freedom-mast field issue was brittle gelcoat circumferential surface cracking over un-cross-linked hoop-glass windings, worst near the gooseneck where bending stress is highest; cracks generally did NOT penetrate the structural carbon — a surface/manufacturing defect, confirming bending stress peaks low on the spar.
findings.value: Surface gelcoat/hoop-glass cracking at high-bending region (gooseneck/lower mast); structural carbon intact
findings.source: Eric Sponberg, 'Freedom Yachts Mast Cracking: Causes and the Cure' PDF

findings.claim: Real megayacht carbon mast laminate scale: ~180 plies at the base dropping to ~20 plies at the tip (drop-offs create the taper), ~50 mm laminate thickness at the base; high-strength intermediate-modulus T800 used for 0deg and +/-45deg plies.
findings.value: ~180 plies base -> ~20 plies tip; ~50 mm base laminate; T800 IM carbon
findings.source: CompositesWorld 'Megayacht Composite Masts Get Smart'

findings.claim: Carbon vs aluminum spar payoff: carbon masts are ~half the weight and roughly twice the strength of aluminum; at 30deg heel a carbon mast gave ~15% more righting moment (lower weight aloft), allowing ~1 m more mast height. GMT has built 1000+ spars 21-140 ft.
findings.value: ~50% weight, ~2x strength vs Al; +15% RM at 30deg heel
findings.source: GMT Composites; smalltridesign Rigging-Mast-Loads; Sponberg

findings.claim: Windsurfer masts (smallest quantified free-standing tapered rotating spar analog) are stiffness-graded by IMCS = Length(cm)^3 / midpoint-deflection(cm) x 216225 under a 30 kg midspan load; IMCS ranges ~11 (soft) to ~36 (stiff race). 'Bend curve' = (3/4-height deflection % - 1/4-height %); lower half always stiffer than upper due to taper.
findings.value: IMCS 11-36; stiffness via 30 kg midspan deflection; lower half stiffer (taper)
findings.source: boards.co.uk; Unifiber windsurf mast guides

findings.claim: Cost crossover: custom carbon free-standing rigs become cost-comparable to stayed rigs only above ~40 ft boat length; below that aluminum wins on price. Rotating-mast bearings are a major cost adder.
findings.value: Cost-comparable above ~40 ft LOA
findings.source: Sponberg state-of-the-art PDF

derived_numbers.quantity: Recommended ultimate factor of safety on laminate strength (operational max-RM load)
derived_numbers.how: Sponberg marine free-standing-spar practice (FoS 3.0) corroborated by wind-turbine blade effective margin: gamma_f (~1.35) x combined gamma_m (~2.45-2.94) = ~3.3-4.0 on coupon strength. The two independent fields bracket 3-4x, so 3.0 is a defensible central value and 2.5-4x the practical envelope requested.

derived_numbers.quantity: Bearing reaction couple force for a rotating mast (per bearing)
derived_numbers.how: Validated against AeroRig measured data: with bury = 1.9 m, deck bearing ~34 t and heel ~28.4 t. The two bearing loads are nearly equal-and-opposite (the small difference is the vertical/compression share), confirming F ~ moment/spacing. Implication: doubling bury roughly halves bearing loads.

derived_numbers.quantity: Tip-deflection limit to adopt (if a hard serviceability limit is wanted)
derived_numbers.value: No fixed marine % limit; if one is imposed, borrow the wind-turbine rule: factored tip deflection <= ~70% of available clearance (<=30% clearance reduction)
derived_numbers.how: Marine spar practice does not enforce a single tip-deflection %; it sizes on strength (FoS 3) and treats deflection as a sail-trim check. The only hard, quantified deflection limit in the analogous-cantilever literature is IEC 61400-1's 30% tip-clearance-reduction-under-factored-load for blades. For a free-rotating wingmast with no tower to strike, a strain/strength-based limit (FoS 3 on max-RM) is the governing criterion, not a geometric tip-deflection %.

Sponberg cites 3-4% as the carbon-mast norm and a 3% minimum in the Scribd design doc; bamboo/natural analogs 5-15%. This is the thin-CFRP-shell local-buckling guardrail; the project's own n>=24 eigen buckling verification (CLAUDE.md) is the rigorous check that supersedes this rule of thumb.

Sponberg 60-80% axial / 20-40% off-axis; smalltridesign braid recipe ~75% / 12% / 13%. Axial carries bending moment; +/-45 carries torsion/shear (critical for a rotating mast driven by the sail couple); 90deg hoop resists ovalization/local buckling and crush at the bearings.

derived_numbers.value: Order of ~9:1 in ply count (e.g. ~180 -> ~20 plies); thickness tapers ~linearly with the falling moment
derived_numbers.how: CompositesWorld megayacht-mast data: 180 plies base, 20 plies tip via ply drop-offs. The cantilever moment falls from max at partners to ~0 at tip, so optimal thickness taper tracks the moment diagram (roughly linear in M for a strength-driven design), not a fixed diameter taper ratio.

derived_numbers.value: ~1/7 of mast height above deck (longer is better for bearing loads)
derived_numbers.how: AeroRig 1-in-7 rule (35 ft mast -> 5 ft bury). Trades off against the F=M/bury bearing-load relation: more bury = lower journal loads but more structure/weight below deck and a longer fixed stub for a rotating design.

derived_numbers.value: Captured inside the safety factor, not a separate explicit DAF in marine spar practice; turbines apply explicit gust load cases with gamma_f ~1.35
derived_numbers.how: Marine free-standing-spar sizing folds gust/dynamic margin into the FoS=3 on the static max-righting-moment load (the righting moment itself caps the load the hull can transmit, providing a natural overload ceiling). Wind-turbine practice instead models discrete extreme-gust load cases (EOG/ECD per IEC 61400-1) and applies gamma_f ~1.25-1.35; a dynamic amplification factor of up to ~2 for a step gust on a lightly-damped cantilever is the conservative bound if modeled explicitly.

open_questions: Two Sponberg source PDFs ('design-engineering-masts.pdf' and the longer state-of-the-art print version) are scanned/image-based and could not be OCR'd here; they likely contain explicit tip-deflection-vs-height curves and the precise gust-factor wording. Worth OCR'ing locally (tesseract) to confirm any numeric tip-deflection % Sponberg actually quotes.

No primary source gave a single canonical free-standing-mast tip-deflection limit as a % of height-above-deck — marine practice appears to be strength-governed (FoS 3) rather than deflection-governed. If a deflection serviceability limit is required for the wingmast project, it should be derived from the project's own aero/strain criteria, not borrowed wholesale; only the wind-turbine 30%-clearance rule is a hard published number and it presumes a tower to strike.

Exact IEC 61400-1 gamma_f / gamma_m / gamma_n breakdown and the 1.485 product figure were inferred from secondary summaries (NREL report, AAU background doc); the AAU ed.4 background PDF returned 503 and should be re-fetched to lock the precise composite material sub-factor table.

Whether the project's closed-form foundation buckling model is calibrated against the 3-4% wall/diameter rule of thumb, or whether the n>=24 eigen verification (per CLAUDE.md) makes that heuristic redundant for sizing — relevant to deciding if the 3% floor should be a hard constraint or just a sanity check.

research.topic: UD carbon/epoxy ply properties (SM T700 + IM tow) and filament-winding manufacturing constraints for a tapered hollow box spar + shell
research.summary: PART 1 — PLY PROPERTIES. The most defensible, fully-traceable ply-level dataset is the NCAMP/NIAR qualification report for the intermediate-modulus system IM7/8552 (report CAM-RP-2009-015 Rev A), which gives RTD lamina allowables normalized to a 0.0072 in (0.183 mm) cured ply thickness: E1≈159 GPa, E2≈9.0 GPa, G12≈4.7 GPa, nu12≈0.32, Xt≈2500 MPa, Xc≈1716 MPa (back-calc from UNC0; direct LC ≈1380 MPa), Yt≈64 MPa, Yc≈286 MPa, in-plane shear S≈53 MPa, all at ~57-60% fiber volume. IM7 fiber itself: 5670 MPa strength, 276 GPa modulus, 1.78 g/cc, 5.2 um filament; HexPly 8552/IM7 typical UD composite 2723 MPa / 164 GPa at 60% Vf. For a STANDARD-MODULUS tow (Toray T700), no single equivalently-rigorous public NCAMP allowable set exists, so I report convergent literature/handbook values for T700/epoxy at ~55-60% Vf: E1≈125-135 GPa, E2≈7.5-9 GPa, G12≈4.5-5 GPa, nu12≈0.31, Xt≈2100-2550 MPa, Xc≈1450 MPa, Yt≈45-76 MPa, Yc≈180-200 MPa, S≈70-90 MPa (in-plane shear strength), density ~1.55-1.60 g/cc, CPT ~0.13-0.20 mm depending on areal weight. A clean teaching/handbook UD carbon/epoxy reference set (Vf 0.55) is E1=130, E2=10, G12=4.5 GPa, nu12=0.28, Xt=1800, Xc=1200, Yt=40, Yc=180, S=70 MPa, rho 1.6 g/cc — good conservative defaults for SM tow. KEY ANISOTROPY POINT: transverse and shear strengths are 25-50x lower than longitudinal, so any off-axis or interlaminar load path is the design driver. PART 2 — MANUFACTURING. (a) A rotating-mandrel filament-winding head MUST reverse direction at each end, so the tow path has to turn around (cross the pole), making true continuous 0-degree fiber geometrically impossible; the practical minimum helical 'low-angle' winding is roughly 5-15 deg on long tubes and effectively cannot go below ~15-20 deg on short/blunt mandrels (the turnaround region forces the local angle up toward 90 deg at the pole). (b) Geodesic paths (Clairaut: r*sin(alpha)=const, geodesic curvature kappa_g=0) are intrinsically slip-free and need no friction; non-geodesic paths add design freedom but rely on friction and are stable only while the slippage coefficient lambda = |kappa_g/kappa_n| stays below the available tow/mandrel friction coefficient mu. Measured/used lambda for CFRP tow is small, typically ~0.2-0.5 (friction experiments, Koussios & Bergsma 2006); exceeding it causes lateral slip or bridging. (c) Because winding can't make true 0-deg fibers, axial UD reinforcement (longerons / spar caps) is added separately: pre-laid axial tow/towpreg or UD tape under the wound layers, or dry UD tow/rod placed in channels and VARTM/infusion-co-consolidated. (d) One-piece tapered mandrels need a draft/taper for friction-free extraction; where geometry prevents pull-off you use collapsible/segmented mandrels or soluble/washout mandrels (water-soluble sand/PVA, plaster, eutectic salt). (e) Co-CURING (cure together, one shot) gives a near-monolithic interface; co-BONDING (cured part + uncured part cured together) and SECONDARY bonding (both cured, joined with adhesive) both create a resin/adhesive-dominated joint plane with NO fibers bridging it, so its strength reverts to interlaminar/bondline allowables (~adhesive lap-shear 20-40 MPa or interlaminar shear ~30-120 MPa) rather than fiber-dominated in-laminate strength. The standard design treatment is a bondline knockdown: design the secondary/co-bond to interlaminar (ILSS/GIC) allowables with an additional knock-down factor (commonly model the joint with cohesive-zone elements at degraded GIC, or simply require the bonded interface never be the critical load path). NOTE the literature is direction-dependent: with a dedicated film adhesive a well-made secondary bond can EXCEED a moisture-degraded co-cure in Mode-I GIC (one DCB study: co-cured ~600 J/m2 vs secondary-bonded ~1000-1200 J/m2), so the 'knockdown' is best understood as 'joint reverts to interlaminar allowables,' not a fixed percentage.

findings.claim: IM7/8552 UD lamina RTD allowables (NCAMP/NIAR, normalized to 0.0072 in CPT): E1 = 22.99 Msi = 158.5 GPa; E2 = 1.30 Msi = 9.0 GPa; G12 = 0.68 Msi = 4.7 GPa; nu12 = 0.316
findings.source: NIAR/NCAMP Hexcel 8552 IM7 Unidirectional Qualification Report CAM-RP-2009-015 Rev A, Table 2-1 Lamina Summary (RTD normalized), p.33 (thyme.ornl.gov/CFCrush/materials/uou/CAM-RP-2009-015...pdf)

findings.claim: IM7/8552 UD lamina RTD strengths (NCAMP): Xt (F1tu from LT) = 362.7 ksi = 2501 MPa; Xc (F1cu from UNC0) = 248.8 ksi = 1716 MPa; Yt (F2tu) = 9.29 ksi = 64.1 MPa; Yc (F2cu) = 41.44 ksi = 285.7 MPa; in-plane shear S (F12 0.2% offset) = 7.76 ksi = 53.5 MPa; short-beam shear 17.13 ksi = 118 MPa
findings.source: NIAR/NCAMP CAM-RP-2009-015 Rev A, Table 2-1, p.33 (RTD normalized column)

findings.claim: Cured ply thickness for the qualified IM7/8552 190 gsm UD tape is 0.0072 in = 0.183 mm; fiber volume ~57-60%, prepreg 35% resin content. (HexPly 8552 datasheet lists Vf = 60%.)
findings.source: NIAR/NCAMP CAM-RP-2009-015 (normalization basis 0.0072 in) + Hexcel HexTow IM7 / HexPly 8552 datasheet (60% Vf)

findings.claim: HexTow IM7 fiber (intermediate modulus, 12K): tensile strength 5670 MPa (820 ksi), tensile modulus 276 GPa (40.0 Msi), density 1.78 g/cc (1780 kg/m3), filament diameter 5.2 um, ultimate elongation 1.8%. Typical HexPly 8552/IM7 UD composite at 60% Vf: 0-deg tensile 2723 MPa / 164 GPa, 0-deg compressive 1689 MPa / 150 GPa, 90-deg tensile 64.1 MPa, short-beam shear 128 MPa.
findings.value: Fiber: 5670 MPa, 276 GPa, 1.78 g/cc, 5.2 um; UD composite 2723 MPa/164 GPa @60% Vf
findings.source: Hexcel HexTow IM7 Carbon Fiber Product Data Sheet (2023), fiber + HexPly 8552 composite tables

findings.claim: Standard-modulus T700/epoxy UD lamina (literature, ~55-60% Vf): representative study values E1=128.6 GPa, E2=7.52 GPa, G12=4.82 GPa, nu12=0.314, Xt=2103 MPa, Yt=76 MPa. NIAR T700GC-12K-31E/#2510 tape: E1~114 GPa, E2~13.8 GPa, G12~5.2 GPa, Vf 53-60%. T700S/epoxy compressive ~1450 MPa, in-plane shear ~136 MPa, 90-deg ~81 MPa (normalized 60% Vf).
findings.source: ResearchGate T700/epoxy lamina tables (figs 358753754 / 46252004 / 369221919); NIAR AGATE T700GC-12K-31E/#2510 UD tape spec; Toray T700S datasheet

findings.claim: Generic handbook UD carbon/epoxy default set at Vf=0.55 (good conservative SM-tow values): E1=130 GPa, E2=10 GPa, G12=4.5 GPa, nu12=0.28, Xt=1800 MPa, Xc=1200 MPa, Yt=40 MPa, Yc=180 MPa, S=70 MPa, density 1.6 g/cc (1600 kg/m3).
findings.source: NTNU TMM4175 composite material-properties reference table (nilspv.folk.ntnu.no/TMM4175/material-properties.html), carbon/epoxy (a)

findings.claim: Cured UD CFRP ply density is ~1.55-1.60 g/cc (1550-1600 kg/m3): fiber ~1.78-1.80 g/cc blended with epoxy ~1.2 g/cc at ~55-60% Vf. Cured ply thickness ranges ~0.13 mm (thin ~150 gsm) to ~0.20 mm (~300 gsm); filament-wound layers are often thicker/less uniform than prepreg tape.
findings.source: Derived from IM7 fiber 1.78 g/cc + epoxy ~1.2 g/cc rule-of-mixtures; NCAMP CPT 0.183 mm at 190 gsm

findings.claim: True continuous 0-degree (purely axial) fibers cannot be laid by rotating-mandrel filament winding: the delivery head must reverse at each end of the mandrel, so the tow must turn around (cross the pole/turnaround). At the turnaround the local winding angle climbs toward 90 deg; the wound layer is a balanced helix (+/-alpha), never a true unidirectional 0-deg layer.
findings.value: 0-deg continuous winding geometrically impossible (head must reverse at poles)
findings.source: Filament-winding pattern/dome literature (winding angle increases to 90 deg toward the pole); US patents 11951674 / 4369934 head-traverse descriptions; Wikipedia Filament winding

findings.claim: Practical minimum helical ('low-angle'/polar) winding angle is roughly 5-15 deg on long slender tubes and effectively cannot go below ~15-20 deg on short or blunt mandrels (for some mandrel designs the band -20 to +20 deg is unwindable). Low-angle helical is commonly cited as <20 deg; high-angle helical 55-85 deg; hoop ~89-90 deg.
findings.value: min helical ~5-15 deg (long), ~15-20 deg unwindable on short mandrels
findings.source: US Patent 11951674 (low-angle helical <20 deg; high-angle 55-85 deg); ResearchGate filament-winding shape optimization (-20/+20 deg unwindable); filament-winding angle-range literature

findings.claim: Geodesic paths obey Clairaut's relation (r*sin(alpha) = const) and have geodesic curvature kappa_g = 0; a tow on a geodesic over a convex surface is inherently slip-free and needs no mandrel friction. Geodesics are the shortest path and the only paths stable without friction.
findings.value: Geodesic: kappa_g=0, r*sin(alpha)=const, slip-free without friction
findings.source: ScienceDirect / NCBI non-geodesic winding papers; ResearchGate slippage-coefficient pattern-generation paper (10.1007/s40430-019-2083-2)

findings.claim: Non-geodesic winding adds design freedom but is stable only while the slippage coefficient lambda = |kappa_g / kappa_n| (ratio of geodesic to normal curvature, equivalently lateral/normal force ratio) remains <= the available tow-mandrel friction coefficient mu; exceed it and the tow slips sideways or bridges over concave regions. A 'semi-geodesic' is a path of constant lambda.
findings.value: Stability criterion: lambda = |kappa_g/kappa_n| <= mu
findings.source: ScienceDirect S1359835X10003106 (slippage coefficient measurement); ResearchGate 326526071 (non-geodesic return trajectory); NCBI PMC7961002

findings.claim: Measured/practical slippage (and dry friction) coefficients for carbon-fiber tow on a mandrel are small, typically on the order of 0.2-0.5; non-geodesic design must keep the demanded lambda below this measured mu. Friction depends on tow tension, bandwidth, speed and resin viscosity.
findings.value: lambda (and mu) typically ~0.2-0.5 for CFRP tow
findings.source: Koussios & Bergsma, 'Friction Experiments for Filament Winding Applications', J. Thermoplastic Composite Materials 2006 (journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0892705706049561); slippage-coefficient measurement papers

findings.claim: Axial / UD longeron (0-deg) reinforcement is NOT made by winding; it is added separately: (i) pre-laid axial tows / towpreg / UD tape placed along the mandrel under or between wound helical+hoop layers, or (ii) dry UD tow or rods seated in channels/grooves and co-infused (VARTM) and consolidated with the wound shell. Filament-wound parts otherwise have strong hoop and helical but weak true-axial properties.
findings.value: Axial UD added via pre-laid axial tow/tape or VARTM-infused dry tow in channels
findings.source: Filament-winding axial-reinforcement patents (8424793, 9156202, 10087042 hoop+helical layering); addcomposites filament-winding guide; spar mandrel taper patents

findings.claim: Mandrel removal: one-piece cylindrical/tapered mandrels are pulled out with extraction gear and REQUIRE a taper/draft to break friction (no slippage plane = no release); where pull-off is impossible, mandrels are collapsible/segmented (disassembled and withdrawn in pieces) or made of soluble/washout material (water-soluble sand/PVA, plaster, eutectic salt) that is dissolved out. Spar mandrels taper wall thickness base-to-tip via added layers or tapered rovings.
findings.value: Tapered (draft for release) vs collapsible/segmented vs soluble (sand/plaster/salt) mandrels
findings.source: CompositesWorld 'Filament winding' (one-piece tapered pulled, collapsible, soluble); US Patent 5306371 (slippage plane needed for release); US3425982A water-soluble mandrels; ScienceDirect 025405849501554X overview

findings.claim: Co-CURING cures both parts together in one shot, forming a near-monolithic resin-continuous interface. Co-BONDING cures a pre-cured part against an uncured part; secondary bonding joins two fully-cured parts with adhesive. Both co-bond and secondary bond create a resin/adhesive joint plane with NO reinforcing fibers crossing it, so joint strength reverts to interlaminar / bondline allowables, not fiber-dominated in-laminate strength.
findings.value: Co-cure = monolithic; co-bond/secondary bond = adhesive interface, no fibers bridging
findings.source: ScienceDirect Co-Curing overview topic page; SciELO/ResearchGate co-bonded vs secondary-bonded Mode-I studies

findings.claim: The structural-design treatment of a secondary/co-bond is to size the bonded interface to interlaminar/bondline allowables with a knock-down, and/or model the interface explicitly with cohesive-zone elements at a degraded fracture toughness GIC. Typical bondline allowables are far below in-laminate values: adhesive lap-shear ~20-40 MPa and interlaminar shear ~30-120 MPa, versus fiber-direction strengths of 1500-2500 MPa. Practice: never let the bonded plane be the critical load path; apply joint knockdown and require cohesive/peel checks.
findings.value: Model joint at interlaminar/bondline allowables (lap-shear ~20-40 MPa; ILSS ~30-120 MPa) with cohesive-zone GIC knockdown
findings.source: Wind-blade spar/web bondline literature (Springer JMST 10.1007/s12206-021-0426-2; Sandia SAND2021-12461); composite bonded-joint cohesive-zone modeling practice

findings.claim: The co-cure-vs-secondary-bond 'knockdown' is direction-dependent and NOT a fixed percentage: with a dedicated film adhesive a well-made secondary bond can EXCEED a moisture-degraded co-cure. One DCB study: co-cured GIC ~600 J/m2 vs secondary-bonded ~1000-1200 J/m2 (secondary bonds failed cohesively, co-cure failed interfacially due to processing moisture). A separate covered/interleaved co-cure study showed co-cure shear 74-88% higher than secondary bonding. So model the joint by its actual interface allowables rather than assuming a universal reduction factor.
findings.value: No universal % knockdown; co-cure vs secondary bond can swing +/- ~70-100% in GIC depending on adhesive, moisture, lamination technique
findings.source: ResearchGate/academia.edu 'Mode I fracture toughness of co-cured and secondary bonded composite joints' (DCB: CC ~600 vs SB ~1000-1200 J/m2); J. Adhesion 2024 covered/interleaved co-cure (+74-88% vs secondary)

64.1 / 2501 -> transverse tension ~39x weaker than longitudinal; drives any off-axis/joint load path

open_questions: No NCAMP-grade public qualification report exists for a filament-wound (wet-wound) T700 system; the T700 ply numbers are aggregated from prepreg/lab literature and a teaching handbook, so wet filament-wound allowables will run lower (higher void content, lower/variable Vf ~50-58%, thicker non-uniform plies) and should be down-rated or coupon-verified for the actual wound process.

The slippage coefficient lambda ~0.2-0.5 is process- and resin-dependent (tension, bandwidth, speed, viscosity, tack); the exact usable value for the chosen resin/tow at the dome/turnaround should be measured (Koussios-type friction test) before committing non-geodesic paths near the spar ends.

The practical minimum winding angle depends on the specific end-cap geometry and turnaround radius of the tapered box spar; a CADfil/CADWIND-type winding simulation is needed to confirm the achievable minimum helix and the turnaround pattern for this particular taper.

The co-bond/secondary-bond knockdown is not a single universal factor; the correct GIC / ILSS to use depends on the actual adhesive (or co-cure resin), surface prep, and moisture control, so a DCB/ENF coupon program on the actual bondline process is needed to set the cohesive-zone allowables for the spar-to-shell joint.

Whether the outer shell should be co-cured to the box spar (monolithic, no joint knockdown but higher tooling/process risk) vs co-bonded/secondary-bonded (lower-risk assembly but joint-allowable-limited) is a structural/manufacturing trade not resolved by the literature alone and should be decided with the project's FEA-in-the-loop joint model.

reference_boat.displacement_loaded_kg: 33324 published / ~38000 design-max assumed (sailboatdata loaded + payload margin)
reference_boat.standard_rig: fractional 9/10 Marconi sloop, carbon in-mast furling main + ~105% genoa
reference_boat.upwind_sail_area_m2: 180 (boat-specs, 100% foretriangle) / 167 (Oyster catalog with in-mast furling). USE 180 m2 as the design driving-force match target.
reference_boat.righting_moment_status: NOT PUBLISHED by builder. Adopted design values below are DERIVED and are the single largest sensitivity in the whole basis.
reference_boat.RM_max_basis: Loaded disp ~38,000 kg x g 9.807 x GZmax ~0.60 m = 224 kN.m; cross-checks the mid of the prompt 150-300 kN.m band. Bracket 150-225 kN.m.

reference_boat.heeling_lever_m: 14.0 (= 12.5 CE above WL + 1.5 CLR below WL)

geometry_targets.configuration: TWIN free-standing fully-rotating CFRP wingmasts, fore-and-aft (streamwise tandem), 50:50 nominal aero load split, independent AoA control.
geometry_targets.airfoil: NACA 0018 soft wingsail (symmetric, t/c = 0.18); pivot/rotation axis at ~0.25c (aerodynamic center) for near-self-trimming balance.
geometry_targets.mast_height_above_deck_m: 22.0 (exposed wing span; vs 26.8 m standard rig - the wing rig is shorter because area is recovered through higher driving-force coefficient, not height).
geometry_targets.CE_above_partners_m: 10.7 (= 12.5 CE above WL - 1.8 deck above WL); this is the operational base-bending moment arm (partners = cantilever root).
geometry_targets.stock_length_deck_to_heel_m: 3.1 (mast bury / bearing spacing) using the AeroRig ~1/7-of-above-deck-height rule (22.0/7 = 3.14 m). Longer bury lowers the two journal-bearing couple loads (F_bearing = M_base / bury).
geometry_targets.total_stock_length_m: ~25.1 (22.0 above deck + 3.1 bury below deck to heel step)
geometry_targets.tip_chord_m: 2.4 (taper ratio 0.6, matching the project NACA-0018 working taper)
geometry_targets.taper: thickness/ply-count tapered base-to-tip tracking the bending-moment diagram (cantilever M falls to ~0 at tip); megayacht analog ~180 plies base -> ~20 plies tip, ~9:1.
geometry_targets.per_mast_wing_area_m2: 75 (= 150 m2 total wing / 2; total from driving-force match to the 180 m2 standard rig). Span/chord = 75/4 ~ 18.75 m aero span; effective AR ~4-5.
geometry_targets.mast_spacing: 1.0-2.0 chord lengths between rotation axes (4-8 m); ADOPT 1.5c = 6.0 m. ~1c maximizes circulation coupling/pointing but risks aft-rig backwinding/buffet; ~2c gives cleaner independence + steering authority. Munk stagger theorem frees streamwise spacing from any induced-drag penalty, so it is chosen for coupling + helm balance + structure.
geometry_targets.rotational_center_offset: rotation axis at 0.25c from leading edge (= 1.0 m aft of LE at the 4 m root chord); set to the cambered operating CoP, not the symmetric 0.25c, to keep residual hinge torque small.
geometry_targets.wall_thickness_to_diameter_floor: >= 3-4% (Sponberg local-shell-buckling guard); superseded as the governing check by the project n>=24 eigen-buckling verification.
geometry_targets.bearing_arrangement: fixed inner stub mast carrying two journal bearings (upper at deck partners, lower at heel step); outer wound mast rotates 360 deg over it. Bearing couple = M_base / bury.

load_cases.name: OP-1 Righting-moment-limited heeling, balanced 50:50 (per mast)
load_cases.description: Steady close-hauled at the heel angle where the boat carries its maximum righting moment. The hull caps the transmissible aero force, so the heeling moment cannot exceed RM_max. Both masts share equally; this is the nominal per-mast design point.
load_cases.inputs: RM_max 225 kN.m; 50:50 split; heeling lever 14.0 m; CE above partners 10.7 m; DAF 1.5 (NBS gust/seaway).
load_cases.base_torque_kNm: 6.4 (design, DAF 1.5) [4.3 static x 1.5; balanced wing, Cm_axis ~ -0.16 at 0.25c+5%c offset]
load_cases.notes: Static per-mast base moment 86.0 kN.m = F_transverse 8.04 kN x 10.7 m. F_transverse = (225/2)/14.0 = 8.04 kN. If keel-stepped through-deck with a longer effective arm (~14.5 m), static rises to ~116.5 kN.m. This is the headline OPERATIONAL case.

load_cases.name: OP-2 Worst single-mast (forward rig fully loaded, aft rig depowered/shadowed)
load_cases.description: Tandem-interaction worst case: in true tandem (spacing >= 1c) the LEADING (forward) rig carries the larger, steadier load while the trailing rig is shadowed and de-rated. Differential AoA control or an aft-rig stall/depower can put a disproportionate share on one mast. Each mast must individually survive a near-full-rig share, not just the 50:50 nominal.
load_cases.inputs: Same RM_max ceiling but load fraction shifted toward one mast: adopt 70:30 (forward:aft) from the tandem CL1/CL2 evidence (leading CL ~0.62-0.66 vs trailing ~0.02-0.23). Worst single mast carries 0.70 x RM_max = 157.5 kN.m heeling; lever 14.0 m; arm 10.7 m; DAF 1.5.
load_cases.base_torque_kNm: 9 (design, DAF 1.5; scaled with the higher per-mast load)
load_cases.notes: The aero ceiling is still the whole-boat RM_max (the hull cannot heel further), so a single mast cannot exceed RM_max if the other is fully unloaded: hard upper bound = 225/14.0 x 10.7 x 1.5 = 258 kN.m at 100:30 -> use 180 kN.m (70:30) as the design single-mast case and 258 kN.m as an absolute single-mast bound. Each spar is sized to the 70:30 case, not the 50:50.

load_cases.name: SURV-1 Bare weathervaned mast, hurricane Cat 3, off-axis side force (GOVERNING)
load_cases.description: Unattended moored/anchored boat, soft sail removed, bare wingmast left free to weathervane in a Cat 3 hurricane (~100 kt sustained). Imperfect weathervaning (vane lag, gust-direction shifts, VIV/galloping) puts the bare mast at a non-zero effective AoA, so the FULL CHORD planform area generates a lift-type side force. This case GOVERNS the structure.
load_cases.inputs: q(100 kt) = 1621 Pa; A_chord = bare-mast planform = 22 m span x ~3.2 m mean chord = ~70 m2 (using the wing chord, not a stripped strut); Cl 1.0-1.2 off-axis; force arm = mid-height ~11 m. (Research used a slimmer 0.7 m bare strut giving A_chord 17.5 m2 / arm 12.5 m -> 426 kN.m; for a soft-wingsail mast whose structural chord is the full ~3-4 m wing chord, the exposed off-axis planform is much larger.)
load_cases.base_bending_moment_kNm: Research basis (17.5 m2, arm 12.5 m, Cl 1.2): 426 kN.m at 100 kt. With gust factor 1.69x on q: ~720 kN.m. ADOPT 450 kN.m design survival base moment (Cl 1.2, no extra gust) as the primary point; 720 kN.m as the gusted upper bound.
load_cases.base_torque_kNm: Significant and sign-uncertain: a stalled/post-stall bare section has an aft-migrated CoP, so axis torque can reach q x A x c x (CoP-0.25c). At 0.40c CoP: ~1621 x 17.5 x 0.7 x 0.15 ~ 3.0 kN.m for the slim strut; scales up with the full wing chord. Treat as a fatigue/buffet driver on the aft mast (large lift fluctuation in tandem-wake data), not just a static peak.
load_cases.notes: GOVERNING CASE: ~2.8x the operational OP-1 moment at 100 kt. The pure-drag idealization (perfect vane, ~6-15 kN.m) is NON-CONSERVATIVE and must NOT be used. Per CLAUDE.md the closed-form foundation buckling model is non-conservative for slam/survival, so this case MUST be eigen-verified at n_levels >= 24 over the lowest 2-3 modes before any spar mass is claimed.

load_cases.name: SURV-2 Bare weathervaned mast, hurricane Cat 5 (sensitivity / upper bound)
load_cases.description: As SURV-1 but at Cat 5 (~137 kt sustained) as an upper-bound sensitivity check. Establishes the worst credible static moment the spar might see.
load_cases.inputs: q(137 kt) = 3042 Pa; A_chord 17.5 m2 (research strut); arm 12.5 m; Cl 1.0-1.2.
load_cases.base_bending_moment_kNm: 666-799 (Cl 1.0-1.2, no extra gust); ADOPT 799 kN.m as the absolute ultimate bound.
load_cases.base_torque_kNm: scales with q; secondary to bending.
load_cases.notes: ~5.3x the operational case. Used as an ultimate sensitivity bound, not the primary design point, unless the owner specifies Cat 5 survivability. Whether the mast can be LOCKED/parked (collapsing survival toward the trivial pure-drag value) is an open design decision that, if allowed, would let SURV-1 stop governing.

load_cases.name: MFG-1 Hoop-wind / cure self-equilibrated prestress + bondline knockdown
load_cases.description: Filament-winding process realities: (a) true 0-deg axial fibers cannot be wound (head reverses at poles), so axial spar caps are pre-laid UD tow/tape under the wound +/-helical and 90-deg hoop layers; (b) the tensioned hoop wrap superposes a self-equilibrated prestress on the skin; (c) any co-bonded/secondary-bonded skin-to-spar joint reverts to interlaminar/bondline allowables (lap-shear ~20-40 MPa, ILSS ~30-120 MPa), ~1 order of magnitude below in-laminate strength.
load_cases.inputs: Non-geodesic winding stability: slippage lambda = |kg/kn| <= mu ~ 0.2-0.5. Min helical angle ~5-15 deg (long) / ~15-20 deg unwindable (short/blunt ends). Bondline GIC by DCB/ENF coupon on the actual process.
load_cases.notes: Not a bending load case but a binding constraint set: the bonded skin-spar interface must NEVER be the critical load path (model with cohesive-zone elements at degraded GIC, or require interlaminar util < 1 with knockdown). Off-axis transverse/shear strengths are 25-50x below longitudinal, so every off-axis or interlaminar path is a potential design driver.

sizing_targets.target: Minimize total CFRP mass of the two wingmast spars (+ wound skin), summed.
sizing_targets.rationale: Mass aloft directly trades against righting moment (carbon vs Al gave +15% RM at 30 deg, ~1 m more height); minimum mass is the project objective and the lever weight aloft amplifies.

sizing_targets.target: <= 2% of exposed span = 0.02 x 22.0 m = 0.44 m, on OPERATIONAL cases (OP-1, OP-2) only.
sizing_targets.rationale: Project established convention (examples 22/35/49 use tip_defl_max_m = 0.02*span). Marine free-standing spars are strength-governed and treat deflection as a sail-trim/luff-curve serviceability check, NOT a survival driver. Deflection must NOT govern survival/ultimate cases (per findings.md V.7 correction: applying the 2%-span serviceability budget to a slam/survival case mis-sizes mass upward).

Project established convention (tip_twist_max_deg = 5.0 across examples). Twist is the binding shadow-price driver in prior medium sizings (-41 kg/deg); aerodynamically it controls per-mast AoA fidelity and the balanced-wing pivot behaviour. The +/-45 plies that carry the rotating-mast torque couple also set twist stiffness.

sizing_targets.target: >= 1.5 on the lowest 2-3 linear-buckling eigenvalues, verified at n_levels >= 24 (NOT the 16x8 sizing mesh).
sizing_targets.rationale: Project convention: buckling_safety_factor = 1.5 in the sizer; eigen verification at converged mesh is mandatory (n=8 is unconservatively overstiff). The closed-form foundation model is well-calibrated for the OPERATIONAL envelope but NON-CONSERVATIVE for slam/survival, so SURV-1/SURV-2 especially must be eigen-verified at n>=24. Failure modes screened: laminate strength, local shell (wall) buckling, global Euler/cantilever buckling.

sizing_targets.target: Tsai-Wu / max-strain reserve R >= 2.0 (allowable = Xt / 2.0) on operational cases.
sizing_targets.rationale: Project established convention (sigma_allow_safety_factor = 2.0, STANDARD_MATERIAL_ISO). Prior sizings show strength rarely binds (Tsai-Wu R ~7 vs 2.0 limit) - the design is buckling/stiffness-governed - so 2.0 is a comfortable operational floor.

sizing_targets.metric: Laminate strength safety factor - ULTIMATE / SURVIVAL
sizing_targets.target: FoS 3.0 on full laminate strength for the survival/ultimate cases (envelope 2.5-4.0).
sizing_targets.rationale: Sponberg marine free-standing-spar practice (FoS 3.0 on max-RM load) bracketed independently by wind-turbine blade effective margin gamma_f(1.25-1.35) x gamma_m(2.45-2.94) = 3.3-4.0 on coupon strength. Two independent fields converge on ~3x. DNV-ST-0412 Cat I would push RF >= 4.5 on design load / >= 3.1 on panel compression as the conservative large-yacht-rig alternative.

sizing_targets.target: Co-bonded/secondary skin-spar interface util < 1 at interlaminar/bondline allowables (lap-shear ~20-40 MPa, ILSS ~30-120 MPa) with a cohesive-zone GIC knockdown; the bonded plane must never be the critical load path.
sizing_targets.rationale: No fibers bridge a secondary/co-bond, so strength reverts ~1 order of magnitude below in-laminate. Knockdown is process-dependent (not a fixed %): set GIC/ILSS from DCB/ENF coupons on the actual bondline.
Sponberg local-shell-buckling guard; sanity floor superseded by the n>=24 eigen check for the binding sizing decision.

basis.derivation_chain:
OPERATIONAL CHAIN (per mast, balanced 50:50, OP-1):
(1) Equilibrium ceiling: max steady heeling moment = max righting moment.
    M_heel,max = RM_max = 225 kN.m  (whole boat).
(2) 50:50 split over two masts:
    M_heel/mast = 225 / 2 = 112.5 kN.m.
(3) Equivalent transverse aero force per mast, over the heeling lever
    (CE 12.5 m above WL + CLR 1.5 m below WL = 14.0 m):
    F_transverse = 112,500 N.m / 14.0 m = 8,036 N = 8.04 kN.
    (Both masts: 16.07 kN = 225,000 / 14.0.)
(4) Cantilever base/partners bending moment (arm = CE above partners,
    12.5 - 1.8 deck = 10.7 m):
    M_base,static = 8.04 kN x 10.7 m = 86.0 kN.m.
(5) Design gust/dynamic factor (Nordic Boat Standard DAF = 1.5):
    M_base,design = 86.0 x 1.5 = 129 kN.m  <-- OPERATIONAL design base bending per mast.
    (Slam/impact DAF 2.0 -> 172 kN.m; keel-stepped arm 14.5 m x1.5 -> 175 kN.m.)
(6) Operational torque (balanced wing): T = q A c |Cm_axis|, q 74.4 Pa, A 90 m2, c 4 m,
    Cm_axis = Cm_ac(-0.10) - CL(1.2)x0.05c offset = -0.16:
    T_static = 74.4 x 90 x 4 x 0.16 = 4.29 kN.m -> DAF 1.5 -> 6.4 kN.m.

WORST SINGLE-MAST (OP-2, 70:30 tandem split):
    M_heel,fwd = 0.70 x 225 = 157.5 kN.m;  F = 157.5/14.0 = 11.25 kN;
    M_base,static = 11.25 x 10.7 = 120.4 kN.m;  x DAF 1.5 = 180 kN.m.
    Absolute single-mast bound (100:30 cannot exceed whole-boat ceiling):
    225/14.0 x 10.7 x 1.5 = 258 kN.m.

SURVIVAL CHAIN (SURV-1, bare weathervaned, off-axis side force - GOVERNING):
    q(100 kt) = 0.5 x 1.225 x (100 x 0.5144)^2 = 1621 Pa.
    A_chord (bare-mast planform, research strut) = H 25 m... using research geometry
        H 25 m, c 0.7 m -> A_chord 17.5 m2, force arm = H/2 = 12.5 m, Cl 1.2:
    M_base = q x Cl x A_chord x arm = 1621 x 1.2 x 17.5 x 12.5 = 425,500 N.m = 426 kN.m.
    With 3-s gust factor 1.69x on q: ~720 kN.m.  ADOPT 450 kN.m design / 720 kN.m gusted.
    Cat 5 sensitivity (SURV-2): q 3042 Pa -> 666-799 kN.m.
    NB: for a soft-wingsail mast whose STRUCTURAL chord is the full ~3-4 m wing chord
    (not a 0.7 m strut), the exposed off-axis planform and hence the moment are LARGER;
    the 426 kN.m is therefore a lower bound on the slim-strut idealization - eigen-verify
    the as-designed exposed section at n>=24.

GOVERNING RATIO: survival 426 / operational 150 (1-reef gust bound) ~ 2.8x at 100 kt;
    799/150 ~ 5.3x at 137 kt. SURVIVAL GOVERNS the spar; OPERATIONAL governs deflection/twist.
assumptions: RM_max = 225 kN.m and RM30 = 175 kN.m are DERIVED, not published by Oyster; they drive every downstream load number linearly and are the single largest sensitivity.

Twin-wingmast geometry (per-mast area 75 m2, root chord 4.0 m, taper 0.6, CE 12.5 m above WL, CLR 1.5 m below WL, 22 m exposed span, deck 1.8 m above WL) is an assumed concept for an unbuilt rig, not measured.

50:50 nominal aero split for OP-1; 70:30 forward:aft adopted for the worst single-mast OP-2 from low-Re tandem-wing CL1/CL2 evidence (Jones/Cleaver/Gursul 2015 at Re 1e5 - magnitudes need re-derivation at design Re).
NBS dynamic amplification factor DAF = 1.5 for operational gust/seaway; 2.0 for slam/impact check. Marine practice otherwise folds gust margin into the FoS, capped naturally by RM_max.
Wing operational point: CL ~1.0-1.2, AoA ~8-10 deg (below NACA-0018 stall ~16-18 deg), whole-rig L/D ~8-10; q ~74 Pa at the heeling-limited operating force (~21 kt apparent).
Survival design wind = Cat 3 ~100 kt sustained (primary), Cat 5 ~137 kt (upper bound); 3-s gust ~1.3x on V => ~1.69x on q.

Ply set: SM-tow defaults E1 130 GPa, E2 10 GPa, G12 4.5 GPa, Xt 1800 MPa, Xc 1200 MPa, Yt 40 MPa, Yc 180 MPa, S 70 MPa, rho 1600 kg/m3 (project T700/epoxy + NTNU handbook); wet-wound allowables run lower (higher void, Vf ~50-58%) and should be down-rated.

Keel-stepped (through-deck) vs deck-stepped is assumed keel-stepped with a two-bearing couple; deck-stepped would add the NBS +50% step penalty and change the base arm (86 vs ~116 kN.m static).

checks.reasoning: RM_max = displacement x g x GZmax. Using design-max disp 38,000 kg x 9.807 x GZmax 0.60 m = 223.6 kN.m, which rounds to the adopted 225. GZmax 0.55-0.65 m is typical for a 5.36 m-beam cruising monohull; the band over plausible disp (33,324 published loaded to 38,000 design-max) and GZ (0.50-0.65) spans 166-242 kN.m, bracketing 225 comfortably. The equilibrium principle (steady aero heeling moment cannot exceed the hull's max righting moment) is sound. CAVEAT: this is DERIVED, not published by Oyster, and is the single largest sensitivity in the whole basis - the basis itself correctly flags this. A heeling moment is conventionally taken at 30 deg (RM30) for rig sizing rather than RM_max at ~50-60 deg, but using the peak RM as a structural force ceiling is the conservative choice and is internally consistent here.
checks.discrepancy: None of substance. My 223.6 vs adopted 225 = 0.6% difference, well inside 25%. The number is sound arithmetically but rests on a derived, unpublished RM curve.

checks.quantity: (b) Per-mast base bending moment (operational, RM-limited, OP-1 50:50)
checks.reasoning: Reproduced the full chain independently: M_heel/mast = 225/2 = 112.5 kN.m; F_transverse = 112,500 N.m / 14.0 m heeling lever = 8,036 N = 8.04 kN; M_base_static = 8.04 kN x 10.7 m (CE above partners) = 86.0 kN.m; x DAF 1.5 = 129.0 kN.m. Also confirmed via the compact ratio form 112.5 x (10.7/14.0) x 1.5 = 129.0. The two distinct arms (14.0 heeling lever including 1.5 m hydro CLR vs 10.7 m structural cantilever arm) are correctly applied - the resisting RM is referenced to the full lever, the base sees only CE-above-partners.

checks.quantity: (c) Survival bending moment, bare weathervaned mast, hurricane Cat 3
checks.independent_value: 426 kN.m (slim-strut Cl 1.2); 720 kN.m gusted x1.69; but ~1250-1500 kN.m if the actual full wing chord is used

checks.quantity: (e) Sail area to match standard-rig drive force

The basis quotes ~18.75 m span and AR ~4-5 by dividing by the ROOT chord 4.0 instead of the mean chord - a minor internal inconsistency in the span/AR descriptors (the 18.75 uses root, not mean). It does not affect the area-match conclusion.

verify.overall: All six critical quantities recompute to within ~6% of the basis (well inside the 25% tolerance) and the governing-case conclusion holds. (f) All serviceability/safety-factor targets (0.44 m tip defl, 5 deg twist, buckling RF 1.5 eigen n>=24, strength FoS 2.0 op / 3.0 survival) are reasonable and corroborated by independent standards. checks.quantity: (c) Survival bending moment, bare weathervaned mast, hurricane (SURV-1, Cat 3)
checks.independent_value: SELF-CONSISTENT with the basis's OWN stated wing-chord planform (22 m span x ~3.2 m mean chord = ~70 m2, arm ~11 m, Cl 1.0-1.2): M = q100 x Cl x A x arm = 1621 x (1.0-1.2) x 70 x 11 = 1250-1500 kN.m, i.e. ~3x the basis's adopted 450 kN.m. With 1.69x gust: ~2100-2530 kN.m. The slim-strut number (17.5 m2, arm 12.5, Cl 1.2 = 426 kN.m) is reproduced exactly but uses an INCONSISTENT 0.7 m chord.

The 450/720 kN.m figures are valid only for a SLIM stripped strut, which contradicts the basis's own soft-wingsail full-chord geometry. RESOLUTION: either (i) commit to a lockable/parkable mast (collapses survival toward pure-drag ~6-15 kN.m and removes survival as governing), or (ii) size to ~1250-1500 kN.m. This is the single most important correction in the basis. The basis's open-questions list does flag this ('426 is a slim-strut lower bound, eigen-verify as-designed planform'), but the headline number must not be the 450.
checks.reasoning: q(100kt)=0.5*1.225*51.44^2=1621 Pa (exact). M=q*Cl*A*arm. The dispute is purely A and arm: basis-stated full-chord A=70 m2/arm=11 gives 1255 kN.m at Cl 1.0; the adopted number used A=17.5/arm=12.5 (a different, slimmer object). For a fat soft wingsail whose structural chord IS the wing chord, the larger planform is the correct one for off-axis side force.

checks.independent_value: Survival GOVERNS the spar; operational governs deflection/twist. Governing ratio is NOT 2.8x but ~10x (self-consistent SURV-1 ~1250 kN.m / OP-1 129 kN.m) if the mast is free-rotating; if lockable, survival collapses and OP-2 (180 kN.m) governs.

But the MAGNITUDE of the governing margin is understated: basis claims ~2.8x (450/150-ish), my self-consistent value is ~10x. The governance call hinges entirely on the open design decision of whether the mast can be locked/parked in a hurricane.

The most consequential unresolved decision is lockability: a parkable mast removes survival as the governing case entirely and makes OP-2 (180 kN.m) govern. This decision should be made BEFORE any spar mass is claimed.
checks.reasoning: Governance = max(design loads). SURV (whether 450 or self-consistent 1250) > OP-2 180 > OP-1 129 in all scenarios where the free mast sees off-axis lift, so survival governs the spar regardless of which survival number is used. Only locking the mast changes the answer.

For equal drive force, the adopted 150 m2 total (vs 180 m2 sloop) implies the wing rig is ~1.20x more efficient per unit area (0.83 area ratio). My independent range: a symmetric soft wingsail credibly gives 1.10-1.35x efficiency (160-135 m2 equivalent); 150 m2 is plausible but slightly optimistic for a THICK t/c=0.18 SOFT wing.

This is in the documented wingsail range (~20-40% area savings from C-Class/AC experience) but optimistic for a fat soft wing (a thick soft section is draggier and lower-CLmax than a thin rigid wing). A more conservative match would be ~160-180 m2. Within the 25% band.

The basis's own open-questions correctly list pinning the per-mast area/CE/chord. Not an arithmetic error, an aero-coefficient assumption.

A self-consistency check confirms the operating point closes: q=74.4 Pa (21 kt apparent), A=150, CL=1.2 -> 13.4 kN side force, comfortably above the 16.07 kN RM ceiling only at slightly higher wind, so the boat is correctly RM-limited at modest wind. Coherent.

checks.independent_value: Tip deflection 2% span = 0.44 m on a 22 m cantilever: squarely in the 1.5-3% free-standing-spar serviceability range (Sponberg/AeroRig). Tip twist 5 deg: reasonable for a rotating wing. SFs: buckling eigen >=1.5 at n>=24, operational Tsai-Wu R>=2.0, survival/ultimate FoS 3.0 (bracketed 2.5-4.0 by Sponberg + turbine gamma_f*gamma_m 3.3-4.0), DNV-ST-0412 Cat I RF>=4.5 as conservative alt -- all individually sound and well-triangulated.
